title: About
text: Transfem enby who likes sports, music, video games, my partner and two of the best cats in the world. Currently studying at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and work as a student reporter for Nebraska Public Media. Just remember Paper and Munchlax love their head scritches.

title: Schema
text:
Full column reference for all 17 tables in this dataset.


One row per race: season, round, circuit, name, date/time, and practice/qualifying/sprint session schedule.







Column
Description




raceId
Unique identifier for the race (primary key).


year
Championship season.


round
Round number within that season.


circuitId
Foreign key to circuits.csv.


name
Official race name, e.g. ‘Monaco Grand Prix’.


date
Race date (YYYY-MM-DD).


time
Race start time (UTC), or if unknown.


url
Wikipedia page for the race.


fp1_date
Free Practice 1 date.


fp1_time
Free Practice 1 start time (UTC).


fp2_date
Free Practice 2 date.


fp2_time
Free Practice 2 start time (UTC).


fp3_date
Free Practice 3 date.


fp3_time
Free Practice 3 start time (UTC).


quali_date
Qualifying session date.


quali_time
Qualifying session start time (UTC).


sprint_date
Sprint race date, or if the weekend had no sprint.


sprint_time
Sprint race start time (UTC), or .






Race classification results: grid position, finishing position, points, laps, race time, fastest lap, and finishing status per driver per race.







Column
Description




resultId
Unique identifier for the result row (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


constructorId
Foreign key to constructors.csv.


number
Car number used in this race.


grid
Starting grid position.


position
Final classified finishing position, or if unclassified (DNF/DSQ/etc).


positionText
Finishing position as text; non-numeric codes like ‘R’ (retired), ‘D’ (disqualified), ‘W’ (withdrew) for unclassified results.


positionOrder
Numeric finishing order for sorting (classified drivers first, by position, then unclassified).


points
Championship points scored.


laps
Laps completed.


time
Race finishing time (leader) or gap to leader, or if not applicable.


milliseconds
Race time in milliseconds, or .


fastestLap
Lap number of the driver’s fastest lap, or .


rank
Rank of this driver’s fastest lap among all drivers in the race, or .


fastestLapTime
Fastest lap time, or .


fastestLapSpeed
Average speed on the fastest lap (km/h), or . Not available from the data source for 2025/2026 races.


statusId
Foreign key to status.csv describing how the race ended for this driver.






Qualifying session results per driver per race, including Q1/Q2/Q3 times and grid position.







Column
Description




qualifyId
Unique identifier for the qualifying result (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


constructorId
Foreign key to constructors.csv.


number
Car number used in qualifying.


position
Qualifying position, which sets the starting grid.


q1
Q1 session lap time, or if not set.


q2
Q2 session lap time, or if the driver didn’t advance to Q2.


q3
Q3 session lap time, or if the driver didn’t advance to Q3.






Sprint race classification results, same structure as results.csv, for race weekends with a sprint format.







Column
Description




resultId
Unique identifier for the sprint result (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


constructorId
Foreign key to constructors.csv.


number
Car number used in the sprint.


grid
Sprint starting grid position.


position
Final classified sprint finishing position, or if unclassified.


positionText
Finishing position as text; non-numeric codes for unclassified results.


positionOrder
Numeric finishing order for sorting.


points
Championship points scored in the sprint.


laps
Laps completed.


time
Sprint finishing time (leader) or gap to leader, or .


milliseconds
Sprint time in milliseconds, or .


fastestLap
Lap number of the driver’s fastest lap in the sprint, or .


fastestLapTime
Fastest sprint lap time, or .


statusId
Foreign key to status.csv describing how the sprint ended for this driver.






Individual pit stop records: which lap, stop number, time of day, and duration per driver per race.







Column
Description




raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


stop
Stop number for this driver in this race (1st stop, 2nd stop, etc).


lap
Lap on which the stop occurred.


time
Time of day the stop occurred.


duration
Pit stop duration in seconds.


milliseconds
Pit stop duration in milliseconds.






Lap-by-lap timing per driver per race (position and time each lap). Does not yet include 2025/2026 data - see README.



Column
Description




raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


lap
Lap number.


position
Driver’s race position at the end of this lap.


time
Lap time.


milliseconds
Lap time in milliseconds.






Championship standings for drivers after each race: cumulative points, position, and wins.







Column
Description




driverStandingsId
Unique identifier for this standings row (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv - standings as of after this race.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


points
Cumulative championship points through this race.


position
Championship standing position.


positionText
Standing position as text.


wins
Cumulative race wins through this race.






Championship standings for constructors (teams) after each race: cumulative points, position, and wins.







Column
Description




constructorStandingsId
Unique identifier for this standings row (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv - standings as of after this race.


constructorId
Foreign key to constructors.csv.


points
Cumulative championship points through this race.


position
Championship standing position.


positionText
Standing position as text.


wins
Cumulative race wins through this race.






Points scored by each constructor in each race, aggregated across both of their drivers.







Column
Description




constructorResultsId
Unique identifier for this row (primary key).


raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


constructorId
Foreign key to constructors.csv.


points
Total points scored by the constructor in this race.


status
‘D’ if the constructor was disqualified from this race, otherwise .






Driver lookup table: name, code, permanent number, date of birth, and nationality.



Column
Description




driverId
Unique identifier for the driver (primary key).


driverRef
URL-safe reference slug for the driver.


number
Permanent car number, or if none assigned.


code
Three-letter driver code, or if none assigned.


forename
Driver’s given name.


surname
Driver’s family name.


dob
Date of birth.


nationality
Driver’s nationality.


url
Wikipedia page for the driver.






Constructor (team) lookup table: name and nationality.







Column
Description




constructorId
Unique identifier for the constructor (primary key).


constructorRef
URL-safe reference slug for the constructor.


name
Constructor/team name.


nationality
Constructor’s nationality.


url
Wikipedia page for the constructor.






Circuit lookup table: name, location, country, and geographic coordinates.







Column
Description




circuitId
Unique identifier for the circuit (primary key).


circuitRef
URL-safe reference slug for the circuit.


name
Circuit name.


location
City or locality.


country
Country.


lat
Latitude.


lng
Longitude.


alt
Altitude in meters. Set to 0 as a placeholder for circuits added after 2024 where this data isn’t available from the source API.


url
Wikipedia page for the circuit.






One row per championship season (year), with a link to that season’s overview.



Column
Description




year
Championship season (primary key).


url
Wikipedia page for that season.






Lookup table of race finishing status codes (e.g. Finished, Retired, Disqualified, Did not start).







Column
Description




statusId
Unique identifier for the status (primary key).


status
Human-readable status text, referenced by results.csv and sprint_results.csv.






Free practice (FP1/FP2/FP3) session results per driver per race, sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers only the 2025/2026 races added by this extension - not available for 1950-2024. Reserve/test drivers who ran practice sessions but didn’t race are not included, since they aren’t in drivers.csv.



Column
Description




raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


session
Which practice session: FP1, FP2, or FP3.


position
Rank within the session by best lap time (1 = fastest).


bestLapTime
Driver’s fastest lap time in this session.


laps
Number of laps completed in this session.






Per-race weather summary (aggregated from minute-by-minute samples), sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers only the 2025/2026 races added by this extension - not available for 1950-2024.







Column
Description




raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


airTempAvg
Average air temperature during the race (°C).


airTempMin
Minimum air temperature during the race (°C).


airTempMax
Maximum air temperature during the race (°C).


trackTempAvg
Average track surface temperature during the race (°C).


trackTempMin
Minimum track surface temperature during the race (°C).


trackTempMax
Maximum track surface temperature during the race (°C).


humidityAvg
Average relative humidity during the race (%).


windSpeedAvg
Average wind speed during the race (m/s).


windSpeedMax
Maximum wind speed during the race (m/s).


rainfall
True if rain was recorded at any point during the race.






Tire strategy per driver per race, sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers only the 2025/2026 races added by this extension - not available for 1950-2024.







Column
Description




raceId
Foreign key to races.csv.


driverId
Foreign key to drivers.csv.


stint
Stint number for this driver in this race (1st stint, 2nd stint, etc).


compound
Tire compound used this stint (SOFT, MEDIUM, HARD, INTERMEDIATE, WET), or if unknown.


startLap
First lap of this stint.


endLap
Last lap of this stint.


lapsOnTire
Number of laps completed on this set of tires (endLap - startLap + 1).

title: The Search For Average Perfection: Formula One
text:
The last 15 years or so have been dull for Formula One.
Red Bull dominance. The Mercedes dynasty. Verstappen terrorizing the podium every weekend. These are stories you’ve heard so much of and stories you are almost certainly tired of.
Granted, there have been years where they action got intense. 2012’s fight between Ferrari and Red Bull. Verstappen and Hamilton fighting to the bitter end in 2021. Even then, those stories become few and far in-between.
Well I, for one, think it’s time we start looking elsewhere.
I no longer care for the McLarens, Mercedes and Red Bulls of the world. Seven drivers championships for Lewis Hamilton? Great. Lando Norris brought McLaren back from the dead? Wonderful. I don’t care.
What I want is a team that’s so good at just being there.
They simply exist. No championship contenders, no teams that probably wish they never took to the track (sorry, Caterham). I just want the best Formula One team to do what they were expected to do.
Let’s go find our team.
We’ll take data from 2010-2026 using this dataset compiling several datasets which track everything from constructors, point totals, circuits, even telemetry data. JolpicaAPI is the one to thank for compiling all the data from Ergast.
For our ideal team, we’ll call them Average F1 Team just to make things simple. Remember, they are perfection. They are the team we want our final team to be.
Furthermore, we’ll merge current teams with their previous names to keep things simple. For example, Racing Bulls will include Toro Rosso and AlphaTauri, Aston Martin will include Force India and the pink-clad Racing Point (maybe the only memorable thing about Racing Point) and Audi will include its history as Sauber/Alfa Romeo/the ugly green thing known as Kick Sauber.
Let’s start by graphing every team’s share of total team points from each season. This allows us to account for changes in the points system and avoid difficult questions, such as “Why did the FIA award double points in Abu Dhabi in 2014?”


Code
library(tidyverse)

✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors




Code
standings_prename <- read.csv("data/archive/constructor_standings.csv")
constructors <- read.csv("data/archive/constructors.csv")
races <- read.csv("data/archive/races.csv")

races_clean <- races |>
  mutate(date = ymd(date), year = year(date)) |>
  select(raceId, name, date, year)

constructors_names <- constructors |>
  select(constructorId, constructor = name)




Code
standings_full <- standings_prename |> 
  left_join(constructors_names |> select(constructorId, constructor), by = "constructorId") |>
  left_join(races_clean |> select(raceId, name), by = "raceId") |>
  left_join(races_clean |> select(raceId, date, year), by = "raceId") |>
  rename(race = name) |>
  select(points, position, constructor, race, date, year)

standings_full |>
  filter(year >= 2010) |>
  distinct(constructor) |>

) 




Code
team_points_share <- standings_full |>
  filter(year >= 2010) |>
  group_by(year, constructor) |>
  slice_max(date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(team_name_history, by = "constructor") |>
  mutate(team = coalesce(team, constructor)) |>
  group_by(year, team) |> 
  summarise(points = sum(points)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(share = points / sum(points)) |>
  ungroup()

averagef1team <- team_points_share |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    avg_share = mean(share)
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = team_points_share, aes(x = year, y = share, group = team), color = "gray", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = averagef1team, aes(x = year, y = avg_share), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = team_points_share, aes(x = year, y = share), color = "darkgray", size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = averagef1team, aes(x = year, y = avg_share), color = "darkred", size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Share of total team points",
       title = "Every team's point share from 2010-2026",
       subtitle = "Average F1 Team is in red, that's who we want to be. Everyone else is in grey. \nYou can probably tell when Mercedes dominated F1.",
       caption = "Chart by Luna Acosta | Data from Ergast, compiled by JolpicaAPI | *2026 is partial") + 
  theme_minimal()









Red is the perfect line. They are Average F1 Racing, and they’ve probably seen “just ok” drivers come and go.
A few things to note: the 2026 data available brings us up to the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. We could very well see Average F1 team move up the ranks now that Kimi Antonelli has locked in the World Driver’s Championship. Good for him! Unfortunately, he and Mercedes are too good for what we’re doing.


Code
closest_teams <- team_points_share |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(season_avg = mean(share), distance = abs(share - season_avg)) |>   
  group_by(team) |>
  summarise(avg_distance = mean(distance), seasons = n()) |>
  filter(seasons >= 5) |>                            
  slice_min(avg_distance, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)


Now I had to remove certain teams, such as HRT, Virgin and Lotus, because their existence does mess with the totals. They’re also just bad. Sorry.
That filter returns five teams that could be Average F1 Team, or at least very, very close: Aston Martin, Alpine, Racing Bulls, Williams and Audi.
Again, this is based off the points share that team had at the end of the season. Those five teams are the closest matches we have, they are now in the race for perfection.
This also includes all their previous teams: for example, Racing Bulls will include Toro Rosso and AlphaTauri, Aston Martin will include Force India and the pink-clad Racing Point (maybe the only memorable thing about Racing Point) and Audi will include its history as Sauber/Alfa Romeo/the ugly green thing known as Kick Sauber.


Code
facet_data <- team_points_share |>
  filter(team %in% closest_teams$team)


This filter allows us to make this facet wrap a little easier, taking the yearly progression of each of our five candidates. For example, we can include Lotus (now Alpine)’s 2012 run, where things got a little too exciting our purposes. Kimi Raikkonen was doing excellently, Romain Grosjean was the first driver in 18 years to get a race ban. Fun stuff, but it puts Alpine on thin ice. We can’t do fun here.


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = averagef1team, aes(x = year, y = avg_share), color = "gray", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = facet_data, aes(x = year, y = share, group = team), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = averagef1team, aes(x = year, y = avg_share), color = "darkgray", size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = facet_data, aes(x = year, y = share, group = team), color = "darkred", size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~team) +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Share of total team points",
       title = "Top 5 and how their point shares compare to Average F1 Team",
       subtitle = "Average F1 Team is in grey, our suspects in red.",
       caption = "Chart by Luna Acosta | Data from Ergast, compiled by JolpicaAPI | *2026 is partial") +
  theme_minimal()









Sorry, Racing Bulls, Williams and Audi. You guys are just too bad for our ranking. Williams could’ve had a fighting chance if they had more fluctuation, but their run from 2018-2024 was influenced by the graces of Nicholas Latifi and Logan Sargeant, two drivers who lacked in pace but exceeded marks when it came to memes.
However, we may have found our target. Enter Aston Martin.
Remember that the closest_teams filter provided us with five teams based on one thing: how far they were from the point share earned by Average F1.
Out of our top five, Aston Martin ranked number one, beating Alpine by one hundredth. You’ll also notice that they follow Average F1 more than the latter, thanks to Alpine being pretty dang good in 2012 and 2013 and pretty dang awful in 2014 and 2016 during the Renault resurgence.
This means that despite the flashes of brilliance from Sergio Pérez, the promise of veteran strength provided by former world champion Fernando Alonso (or maybe despite Lance Stroll), Force India/Racing Point/Aston Martin has proven to be the most average F1 team we have on the grid.
Let’s explore this even further.


Code
aston_average <- team_points_share |>
  filter(team == "Aston Martin") |>
  left_join(averagef1team, by = "year")

alpine_average <- team_points_share |>
  filter(team == "Alpine") |>
  left_join(averagef1team, by = "year")


In this step chart, we are gonna compare Aston Martin’s points share progression from 2010-2026 to Average F1. No team’s perfectly average, no matter how much I wish a team could be, so the British squad could out-compete Average F1 in certain years.
However, the chart will show just how close to perfection AM has gotten over the last 16-ish years.
I’ll even throw in Alpine, our second-place candidate, just so I can show you how close this was.


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_step(data = alpine_average, aes(x = year, y = share), color = "lightblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_step(data = averagef1team, aes(x = year, y = avg_share), color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_step(data = aston_average, aes(x = year, y = share), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2025.7, y = 0.085, label="Average F1") +
  annotate("text", x = 2026, y = 0.045, label="Alpine") +
  annotate("text", x = 2025.6, y = 0.0, label="Aston Martin") +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Share of season's total points",
       title = "Aston Martin vs. Average F1",
       subtitle = "Aston Martin competes with Average F1 more than Alpine, who's *just* too good for us",
       caption = "Chart by Luna Acosta | Data from Ergast, compiled by JolpicaAPI | *2026 is partial") +
  theme_minimal()









Alpine, if your Lotus outfit was just a tad bit worse from 2012-2013, you would’ve won the award for the team closest to perfection. One thing you do have over Aston is that you were nearly right on the mark in 2011.
Alpine, almost always there, story of their Lotus life. Not so much now, much to the chagrin of the French fanbase.
Aston beats Alpine in consistency. Their points shares between the 2014 and 2017 seasons match that of Average F1 better than any other team on the grid. Even when they went up and down in the early 2020s, they were near the mark more times than Alpine.
It’s not perfection. Perhaps with a sport as volatile as motorsport, we may never get that average perfection we’re looking for.
But the team clad in beautiful British Racing Green, the team that spent years fighting for an identity (and nearly found one with the success of Checo), instead sat exactly where we wanted a team to be.
Aston Martin is the most average F1 team since 2010.

title: Changelog
text:
Regenerated SCHEMA.md to include tire_stints.csv, weather.csv, and practice_results.csv (it had gone stale after those tables were added).





Added practice_results.csv: FP1/FP2/FP3 session results (best lap time, laps, rank) per driver per race, sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers the 2025/2026 races only. Reserve/test drivers who only ran practice are excluded.





Added weather.csv: per-race weather summary (air/track temp, humidity, wind, rainfall flag), sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers the 2025/2026 races only.





Added tire_stints.csv: tire compound and stint length per driver per race, sourced from official F1 live timing via FastF1. Covers the 2025/2026 races only.





Added SCHEMA.md (standalone column reference) and this changelog.





Backfilled lap_times.csv for all 35 completed 2025/2026 races (+39,357 rows). Previously skipped due to Jolpica API rate limiting; fetched race-by-race on a slower schedule this time.





Added per-file and per-column descriptions across all 14 tables.
Fixed results.csv/sprint_results.csv position column to correctly use \N for unclassified (DNF/DSQ/etc) drivers, matching the base dataset’s convention. This also corrected positionOrder sorting for those rows.





Initial release: extended the base Formula 1 World Championship (1950-2020) dataset with the full 2025 season (24 races) and every completed 2026 round through the Hungarian Grand Prix (round 11).
New entities added: 18 drivers, 2 constructors (Audi, Cadillac), 1 circuit (Madring), 2 status codes (Lapped, Did not start).
lap_times.csv intentionally left unchanged for 2025/2026 (see v3).
